bib.title: Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable,Navigable, and Editable

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Harness Handbook: Making Evolving Agent Harnesses Readable, Navigable, and Editable", Ruhan Wang, Yucheng Shi, Zongxia Li, et al. (Tencent HY LLM Frontier, Indiana Univ., etc.), arXiv:2607.13285v1 [cs.AI], preprint, 14 Jul 2026.

COVERAGE: 29 of 29 pages; 100012 of 100012 chars. Body, appendices A, B, C, E and the contents of appendix D were read in full. Appendix D prompt templates (about 20k chars, from char 76066 to 96391) were only sampled: the first ~3.4k chars (D.1.1 function classifier) are read, the rest skipped as prompt boilerplate. References were skimmed. Figure pixels were not viewed; figure data came from extracted text.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Behavior localization (finding every code site a behavioral change request touches) is the bottleneck in evolving agent harnesses. The paper proposes a behavior-organized, source-linked "Handbook" (L1 system overview, L2 stage/component, L3 unit with locators, plus a cross-stage state-register view) built by static analysis plus LLM structuring.
  number: none
  setup: argument and design, Sec 1 and 3
  quote: "Behavior localization is therefore a central bottleneck in harness evolution."
  where: abstract, p1

- claim: Handbook-assisted planning beats exploring the repo directly on plan-quality win rate, on both harnesses.
  number: Codex 38.3% vs 28.3% (+10.0); Terminus-2 45.6% vs 26.7% (+18.9)
  setup: planner DeepSeek-V4-Pro (NexAU, read-only); 30 requests per harness; 3 LLM judges (GPT-5.5, Opus 4.8, DeepSeek-V4-Pro); a win needs a score gap of at least 3 points on a weighted 0-100 score (0.5 Loc + 0.25 Scope + 0.25 Reasoning); only two harnesses
  quote: "38.3% versus 28.3% on Codex and 45.6% versus 26.7% on Terminus-2."
  where: Sec 4.2.1, p8

- claim: It also used fewer planner tokens, so the gain is not from a bigger budget.
  number: Codex 0.102M to 0.089M tokens/request (-12.7%); Terminus-2 0.058M to 0.053M (-8.6%)
  setup: same as above; token count includes handbook and source context
  quote: "Average use falls from 0.102M to 0.089M tokens per Codex request (12.7%) and from 0.058M to 0.053M tokens per Terminus-2 request (8.6%)."
  where: Sec 4.2.1, p9

- claim: Against reference plans from stronger models, the handbook raises Recall, Precision and F1 in all 24 comparisons, and cuts complete misses ("Wrong").
  number: F1 gains 5.0 to 18.8 points; Terminus-2 file F1 84.7 (Opus ref) and 89.3 (GPT-5.5 ref); Codex Wrong vs Opus ref 37.0 to 14.8 file, 44.4 to 18.5 symbol
  setup: references are plans written by Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, not ground-truth edits. Codex gains vs the GPT-5.5 reference are small (file recall +0.4, Wrong 0.0).
  quote: "all 24 Recall, Precision, and F1 comparisons are higher for the Handbook-Assisted arm, with F1 gains ranging from 5.0 to 18.8 points."
  where: Sec 4.2.2 and Table 1, p9

- claim: Gains hold across request types and difficulty levels, and are largest for hard-to-keyword-search cases.
  number: type gains 16.3 to 33.3 points (Terminus-2 Search-Hostile +33.3; Codex Query +26.7); difficulty gains 3.7 to 33.3 points, not monotonic
  setup: 10 requests per type per harness (30 split three ways), so slices are very small
  quote: "All six harness-by-type comparisons favor the Handbook-Assisted arm, with gains ranging from 16.3 to 33.3 percentage points."
  where: Sec 4.2.3, p10

- claim: Per-dimension gains are modest, and Localization is the biggest only on Terminus-2.
  number: Terminus-2 +12.2 Loc, +6.7 Scope, +4.5 Reasoning; Codex +2.2, +1.1, +3.3
  setup: averaged over 3 judges
  quote: "The respective gains are 12.2, 6.7, and 4.5 points on Terminus-2, and 2.2, 1.1, and 3.3 points on Codex."
  where: Sec 4.2.1, p9

- claim: Design rule: the repo stays the authority. Every L3 locator must resolve to current code or the entry is frozen and excluded; the handbook stores a location index, not source. Each non-empty diff triggers a scoped resync (fingerprints ignore line numbers; the LLM is used for only four semantic steps).
  number: none
  setup: design, Sec 3.1 and 3.3.3; App. B
  quote: "If a locator cannot be revalidated, its entry is frozen and excluded from localization until it is refreshed. The repository therefore remains the authority for implementation details."
  where: p4

- claim: BGPD (Behavior-Guided Progressive Disclosure) workflow: read L1/L2 to pick stages, follow the state-register view to add coupled stages, open only the relevant L3 entries, expand along the call graph, then verify against the live repo. Only verified sites enter the plan.
  number: none
  setup: Sec 3.3.1, App. B.1
  quote: "The handbook thus guides the search, while the repository remains the basis for the edit plan."
  where: p6

- claim: The state-register view (each shared state variable with ALL read/write sites) is what surfaces scattered sites. In the walkthrough, the register showed initialization and per-run reset had to change with the loop. A single Boolean flag was found in 7 occurrences across 3 functions.
  number: 7 occurrences (single example)
  setup: one trace, Terminus-2 case Q1 (triple completion confirmation); anecdotal
  quote: "the register's write sites reveal that initialization and per-run reset must change together with the loop, not just the obvious return branch."
  where: App. E, p28

- claim: Scale of the two harnesses and the resulting handbooks.
  number: Terminus-2 6 files, 103 functions, 20 stages, 106 L3 entries, 10 registers; Codex 2,267 files, 34,363 functions, 140 stages, 2,267 L3 entries, 62 registers
  setup: Terminus-2 uses function-as-leaf (Python); Codex uses file-as-leaf (Rust). No handbook build cost is reported.
  quote: "The two repositories differ by roughly two orders of magnitude in files, functions, and call edges"
  where: App. C Table 2, p19

LIMITS
- Only two harnesses, 30 requests each (10 per type), one planner model (DeepSeek-V4-Pro). Judges are LLMs, and reference plans are LLM-written.
- The paper reports no significance tests or confidence intervals, and no execution of the edits. It scores plans, not working patches.
- Handbook construction and resync cost (LLM calls, time) is not counted in "fewer tokens". Planner tokens only.
- Codex gains are small on several metrics (+1.1 Scope, +0.4 file recall vs GPT-5.5).
- Not tested against simpler baselines (repo maps, AGENTS.md, code search). The baseline is raw exploration only. The related-work claim that existing representations are "implementation-centric" is asserted, not compared.
- The conclusion's "weaker planner matches stronger models" rests on agreement with references, not on a stronger-planner arm.
- Future work (self-evolving harness, behavior auditing) is only proposed.
- Handbook is for harness codebases, but the method is generic to repos.

BUILDS ON: Progressive disclosure and repo maps/indexing/memory (refs [16-20, 29, 30], e.g. Wang et al. 2025 "Improving code localization with repository memory", Cherny-Shahar 2026 "Repository intelligence graph", Pan et al. 2026 "Natural-language agent harnesses"); harness-as-software (Code as Agent Harness, Ning et al. 2026); OpenAI harness engineering (Lopopolo, Feb 2026); Anthropic harness design (Rajasekaran, Mar 2026); Terminus-2 / Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al. 2026); Codex (OpenAI 2025); NexAU (Nex-AGI 2025); OpenHands, SWE-agent, AutoGen; hierarchical summarization for repos (Oskooei 2025).

RELEVANCE TO NOTE 09 (my reading, as a factual comparison)
- The note says: knowledge sits next to code, the entry file is a router with progressive disclosure, docs decay (knowledge decay), and "Make the map enforceable". Note 09 does not mention that a repo map can be generated and kept in sync mechanically. The paper's resync-after-diff rule and frozen-if-locator-fails rule are a concrete form of "update with code" and "stale doc is worse than none".
- The paper's evidence is about generated behavior-to-code maps for localization. It is NOT about AGENTS.md files and should not be cited as evidence on entry-file length. Gloaguen et al. (already in the note) found generated context files did not help, so the two sources look to conflict. The difference is that the Handbook is a navigable L1-L3 tree with verified locators, not a flat overview file. The paper does not discuss Gloaguen.
- The SKILL.md manifest (Fig. 6) is a progressive-disclosure router for the map. Its steps ("read overview first", "read index", "read registers", "open stage", "open the real code", "plan must account for every site") match the note's router pattern.

CODE (verbatim, App. C Fig. 6, p21)
```
---
name: <harness>-handbook
description: >-
Structural map of the harness, derived from its code. Use it when planning a
change to find EVERY code site the change must touch -- it maps the code
stage-by-stage and lists every state register together with all of its
read/write locations. Consult it before finalizing a plan so that scattered or
non-obvious sites are not missed.
---
```
Key manifest rule: "Your plan must account for every site the handbook surfaced." and "you verify every location against the real code before planning it."

FIGURES (not viewed as images; from extracted text)
- Fig 1 (p4): three-level L1-L3 hierarchy plus state-register navigation pane; fastest picture of the representation.
- Fig 2 (p5): construction pipeline: Phase I static facts, Phase II behavioral organization with propose-review loop, Phase III synthesis.
- Fig 3 (p8): win rates and token cost per harness and per judge. Fig 4: per-dimension win rates. Fig 5 (p9): win rate by request type and difficulty.
- Table 1 (p9): all localization metrics. Fig 6 (p21): SKILL.md manifest.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction was clean text, but figure data is scrambled (axis ticks), so figure numbers are not usable beyond what the body text states. Appendix D prompts (from D.1.1 onward) were not fully read. "Opus 4.8", "GPT-5.5" and "DeepSeek-V4-Pro" are as printed in the paper. I did not edit anything.
